This module shows you how to organize your farm according to your needs and your land.

pages.title: A good design makes use of every corner of the farm: corners, edges, the backs of buildings, spaces under certain
pages.text:
structures, or areas near fences are not wasted space.

They can be used for compost bins, educational displays, tool storage, organic material storage, sheltered

nurseries, medicinal plants, or useful hedges (windbreaks, fodder, wood production). When used effectively, these

spaces free up central areas for cultivation and improve traffic flow and the overall organization of the farm.

pages.title: Good space organization allows you to work faster and with less effort. The goal is to reduce unnecessary
pages.text:
movement and make everyday tasks easier.

Here are a few principles to apply:

Place water, compost, and tools in close proximity to the growing beds.

Organize work areas in a logical and compact manner.

Provide clear paths that are accessible on foot or by wheelbarrow.

Create simple and visible storage spaces.

pages.title: ZONE 0
pages.text:
ZONE 1

ZONE 2

ZONE 3

Zoning means placing each element of the farm according to how often it is used: the more often it is used, the

closer it is.

Here is a typical layout:

Zone 0: central management, storage, and rest area.

Zone 1: intensive cultivation beds requiring daily monitoring.

Zone 2: long-cycle crops, fruit trees, green manure, compost bin.

Zone 3: organic matter storage or extension space.

For example, in practice:

The 10 bed plots are grouped around zones 0 and 1 to limit movement.

The compost bins and water reserves are accessible to several plots.

Trees on permanent beds at the edge provide shade, protection, and production.

pages.title: Taking climate into account in your organization
pages.text: Taking climate into account in your organization

Once the space is well organized, you need to think about the orientation and protection of crops from the climate.

1. Orient the beds according to the sun's path (north-south or east-west depending on the crops).

2. Protect sensitive areas (nurseries, lettuce, etc.) with natural shade or shade nets.

3. Protect against wind and dust with windbreaks or trees along the edges.

4. Manage rainwater with ditches, raised beds, or good drainage.

5. Install small shelters for tools, young plants, or seeds.

Considering these elements from the design stage ensures good crop growth and limits losses.

pages.title: SHELTER AND STORAGE
pages.text:
ACCESSIBLE WATER SOURCES

Once the space has been organized and protected, you need to plan for the structures that are essential to the

smooth running of the micro-farm.

Storage: Seeds and tools protected from moisture. Harvests to be kept in the shade before sale or processing.

Tool shelters: Large tools under a simple roof. Small tools hung up or stored so they remain accessible.

Water: Main reserve + small water points close to crops.

pages.title: COMPOST BIN
pages.text:
FRUIT TREES

CLOSING

Compost: 1 compost bin for a small farm, 2 for a medium-sized farm, up to 4 for a large farm. It is advisable to

place compost bins slightly away from living and working areas to avoid nuisances related to odors, insects, or foot

traffic, while ensuring that they remain easily accessible from growing areas.

Fruit trees: Plant one row at the front edge of the crops and another at the end of the plot (spaced 1.5 m apart).

They provide shade, fruit, and protection.

Fence: Sturdy, well-placed, with an easy-to-access gate.

Anticipating these elements avoids costly reorganizations and makes the system run more smoothly from the start.

There is no single right model: how a farm is organized depends on its objectives, resources, and land. Here are four

concrete examples, which can be adapted as needed.

The important thing is to design a coherent, functional, and scalable system that is tailored to your circumstances.

pages.title: A good design is a coherent and practical system. It simplifies your daily work.
pages.text:
Efficiency: organize the space to reduce movement and keep tools, water, and compost always within reach.

Adaptability: design with climate, available resources, and terrain constraints in mind.

Scalability: think of a flexible design that can grow or adjust over time.
